summary: The bill amends the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage in steps to $25 per hour (with large employers reaching it first by 2031 and smaller ones by 2038), then automatically index it each year to two-thirds of the national median hourly wage, while phasing out all subminimum wages for tipped, youth, disabled, and incarcerated workers.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise minimum wages across employer categories and phases out subminimum wages. It contains no provisions that authorize, appropriate, or alter any federal expenditures, entitlements, or agency budgets. Any secondary fiscal effects (e.g., possible changes in public-assistance outlays) are speculative and not addressed in the text.
The legislation contains no tax-rate changes, credits, deductions, or revenue provisions of any kind.
No provisions address health insurance, Medicaid, Medicare, provider regulation, or any aspect of the healthcare system.
The bill is silent on firearms, background checks, or gun-related regulations.
No immigration, visa, border, or work-authorization language appears in the text.
The bill does not mention reproductive health services, funding restrictions, or abortion access.
No defense-authorization, military pay, or Department of Defense spending provisions are present.
The legislation contains no environmental, energy, or regulatory provisions related to climate or natural resources.

Section 2 findings state that a higher minimum wage “reduces reliance on public assistance.” This is an explicit, albeit secondary, policy rationale, but the bill itself does not amend any welfare, SNAP, housing, or other safety-net statutes.
No education funding, school-choice, or federal-education-policy language is included.
The bill does not address controlled substances, decriminalization, or enforcement.

Section 10 extends FLSA coverage to incarcerated workers employed by public or private correctional facilities and bars certain deductions from their wages. This constitutes a modest criminal-justice reform expanding labor protections inside the correctional system.
No tariff, trade-agreement, or import/export provisions exist.
The bill neither authorizes new deficit spending nor contains debt-ceiling or fiscal-consolidation measures.
No provisions address sexual orientation, gender identity, or related civil-rights protections.
The legislation does not mention foreign assistance, State Department programs, or international spending.
No election-administration, voting-access, or campaign-finance content is present.
The bill contains no data-privacy, platform-regulation, or technology-policy provisions.

The core purpose is to strengthen worker protections by mandating higher minimum wages, eliminating subminimum-wage categories, and extending coverage to previously excluded groups (tipped, youth, disabled, and incarcerated workers). These are classic labor standards that favor employees over employer flexibility.
No religious-exemption, conscience-clause, or anti-discrimination language appears.
